lessons.title: Macbeth: plot and structure
lessons.summary: Trace the story of Macbeth act by act and learn how Shakespeare shapes it as a five-act tragedy with a clear rise and fall.
objectives: I can retell the main events of Macbeth in the correct order, act by act.
I can explain how the play follows the structure of a tragedy: exposition, rising action, climax, falling action and catastrophe.
I can identify key turning points and explain why they matter to the play as a whole.
I can use plot knowledge to support points in an exam answer without simply retelling the story.

activities.title: Act 1: the prophecy and the plan
activities.content:
## Act 1: the prophecy and the plan

The play opens on a storm-blasted heath with three **witches** planning to meet Macbeth. Their chant, *"Fair is foul, and foul is fair"* (Act 1 Scene 1), warns us that nothing in this world will be quite what it seems.

We then hear of **Macbeth** before we see him: a bleeding captain describes how he cut down the rebel Macdonwald and helped defeat Norway. King **Duncan** rewards him with the title **Thane of Cawdor**, taken from the traitor who held it before.

On the heath the witches greet Macbeth with three titles: Thane of Glamis (which he already is), Thane of Cawdor (which he is about to be) and *"king hereafter"*. They tell **Banquo** his descendants will be kings, though he will not.

When the Cawdor prophecy comes true, Macbeth's ambition wakes up. Duncan then names his son **Malcolm** heir, which Macbeth sees as an obstacle. **Lady Macbeth** reads his letter, fears he is too kind to seize the crown, and calls on spirits to *"unsex me here"* (1.5). When Duncan arrives at their castle, Macbeth wavers, but she shames him into agreeing to murder the king that night.

activities.title: Turning a plot event into an exam point
activities.content:
**Retelling** the plot gets no marks on its own. The trick is to use an event as **evidence** for a point about character, theme or structure.

| Plot event | Weak (retelling) | Strong (using the event) |
|---|---|---|
| Duncan names Malcolm heir (1.4) | "Then Duncan makes Malcolm Prince of Cumberland." | "Shakespeare places Malcolm's promotion immediately after the prophecy is half-fulfilled, so Macbeth's aside about *'black and deep desires'* shows ambition curdling into intent the moment a barrier appears." |
| Lady Macbeth reads the letter (1.5) | "Lady Macbeth reads the letter and decides to kill Duncan." | "By having Lady Macbeth react to the letter alone on stage, Shakespeare reveals her ruthlessness before the couple meet, so the audience already fears her influence." |

Notice the strong versions say **what Shakespeare does** and **why it matters**, and quote briefly.

question.text: Put these Act 1 events in the order they happen in the play.
question.hint: The witches speak to Macbeth before he learns that he has actually become Thane of Cawdor.
question.explanation: The captain reports the battle, then the witches meet Macbeth and Banquo, then Ross brings the news about Cawdor, then Duncan names Malcolm heir, and finally Lady Macbeth reads the letter.
order: The bleeding captain describes Macbeth's bravery in battle
The witches greet Macbeth as Thane of Cawdor and future king
Ross arrives and tells Macbeth he is now Thane of Cawdor
Duncan names Malcolm as Prince of Cumberland
Lady Macbeth reads Macbeth's letter and calls on the spirits

activities.title: Acts 2 and 3: the murder and its consequences
activities.content:
## Act 2: the murder

Alone at night, Macbeth sees a vision: *"Is this a dagger which I see before me?"* (2.1). He kills Duncan off stage, then returns shaken, carrying the daggers he should have left with the sleeping guards. Lady Macbeth takes them back and smears the guards with blood.

A drunken **Porter** jokes about being the gatekeeper of hell, a moment of dark comedy that delays the discovery. **Macduff** finds the body. Macbeth kills the guards, claiming rage, and Duncan's sons **Malcolm** and **Donalbain** flee, which makes them look guilty. Macbeth is crowned at Scone.

## Act 3: the crown brings no peace

Macbeth now fears **Banquo**, whose sons were promised the throne. He hires murderers; Banquo is killed but his son **Fleance** escapes. At the coronation feast Banquo's **ghost** appears to Macbeth alone, and Lady Macbeth has to send the guests away.

Macbeth admits he is *"in blood / Stepp'd in so far"* (3.4) that going back would be as hard as going on. He decides to visit the witches again. We also learn Macduff has gone to England to seek help from Malcolm. The banquet scene is often seen as the **climax**: the highest point of Macbeth's power, and the moment it begins to crumble.

activities.title: Spotting a structural turning point
activities.content:
**Question:** Why is Fleance's escape (3.3) such an important moment?

**Model reasoning:**

1. **What happens:** the murderers kill Banquo, but Fleance runs into the dark.
2. **Why it matters for plot:** the witches' prophecy about Banquo's line stays alive, so Macbeth's crown is never secure.
3. **Why it matters for structure:** it is the first thing Macbeth cannot control. Before this, every plan worked; from here on, everything goes wrong. It marks the shift from **rising action** to **falling action**.
4. **Why it matters for meaning:** it suggests fate cannot be cheated, however much blood is spilled.

A single escaped boy changes the whole direction of the play. Look for these **hinge** moments when you revise: the first prophecy, Duncan's murder, Fleance's escape, the apparitions, and Lady Macbeth's death.

question.text: Why do Malcolm and Donalbain flee Scotland immediately after Duncan's murder?
question.hint: Think about who would be suspected next if the murderer struck again.
question.explanation: They fear that whoever killed their father will come for them too, and they do not trust anyone in the castle. Their flight makes them look guilty, which lets Macbeth take the throne.

options.text: They fear they will be the next victims and do not know whom to trust
They have been named as the murderers by Macduff
options.feedback: Macduff does not accuse them; their flight makes others suspect them.

options.text: They are going to raise an army with the witches' help
Lady Macbeth orders them to leave

activities.title: Acts 4 and 5: the fall
activities.content:
## Act 4: the apparitions

The witches show Macbeth three **apparitions**: an armed head (beware Macduff), a bloody child (no man born of woman can harm him) and a crowned child holding a tree (he is safe until Birnam Wood moves to Dunsinane). Then a line of eight kings appears, with Banquo's ghost pointing at them as his descendants. Macbeth responds by ordering the slaughter of Macduff's wife and children.

In England, Malcolm tests Macduff's loyalty by pretending to be wicked. When Macduff learns his family has been murdered, his grief turns to a desire for revenge.

## Act 5: the catastrophe

Lady Macbeth, once so controlled, now sleepwalks, rubbing her hands and crying *"Out, damned spot!"* (5.1). The English army cuts branches from Birnam Wood as camouflage, so the wood really does seem to move. Macbeth hears of his wife's death and reflects that life is *"a tale / Told by an idiot"* (5.5).

He fights on, killing Young Siward, until he meets Macduff, who was *"from his mother's womb / Untimely ripp'd"* (5.8): born by caesarean, so not "of woman born" in the ordinary sense. Macbeth is killed, and Malcolm is hailed as king. Order is restored, and the play ends where it began: with a battle and a traitor's head.

question.text: Match each apparition from Act 4 Scene 1 to the message it gives Macbeth.
question.hint: Each apparition's appearance hints at its message: the armour, the blood, the tree.
question.explanation: The armed head warns him to beware Macduff. The bloody child says no one of woman born can harm him. The crowned child with a tree says he is safe until Birnam Wood comes to Dunsinane.

pairs.right: Beware Macduff, the Thane of Fife
No man born of a woman can harm Macbeth

pairs.left: A crowned child holding a tree
pairs.right: Macbeth is safe until Birnam Wood moves to Dunsinane

activities.title: The shape of a tragedy
activities.content:
## The five-act tragedy

Shakespeare's tragedies usually follow a recognisable shape. Knowing it helps you talk about **structure**, which examiners reward under AO2.

| Stage | In Macbeth |
|---|---|
| **Exposition** (Act 1) | Witches, battle, prophecy, Lady Macbeth's plan |
| **Rising action** (Acts 2–3) | Duncan's murder, coronation, Banquo's murder |
| **Climax** (Act 3 Scene 4) | The banquet: Macbeth at the peak of his power, but publicly falling apart |
| **Falling action** (Act 4) | Apparitions, the Macduff murders, Malcolm's army |
| **Catastrophe** (Act 5) | Lady Macbeth's death, Macbeth's defeat, Malcolm crowned |

**Useful structural ideas**

- **Tragic hero**: a great man with a fatal flaw (his *hamartia*, ambition) whose downfall we watch.
- **Peripeteia**: the reversal of fortune, when success turns to disaster.
- **Cyclical structure**: the play starts and ends with a battle, a traitor beheaded and a new Thane of Cawdor honoured. Macbeth becomes the very traitor he replaced.
- **Pace**: it is Shakespeare's shortest tragedy. The murder happens by Act 2, and the speed mirrors how quickly ambition consumes Macbeth.

question.text: Complete the sentences about the structure of the play.

metadata.blanksText: Macbeth is a tragedy in ___ acts. The banquet scene in Act 3 is often described as the ___ of the play, and Macbeth's fatal flaw, or hamartia, is his ___.

question.hint: Think about how many acts Shakespeare's plays have, the technical word for the peak of the action, and what drives Macbeth to kill.
question.explanation: The play has five acts. The banquet is the climax, the peak from which Macbeth falls. His hamartia is ambition.

activities.title: Writing about structure in an essay
activities.content:
Here is a short paragraph that uses **plot and structure** to answer the question *"How does Shakespeare present the consequences of Macbeth's ambition?"*

> Shakespeare structures the play as a rapid rise followed by a long fall. Macbeth gains the crown by the end of Act 2, but the remaining three acts show that the crown gives him nothing but fear. The banquet in Act 3 Scene 4 is the turning point: he sits at the head of the table as king, yet the ghost only he can see exposes his guilt in front of the court. From this point the structure works against him. Fleance has escaped, Macduff has fled, and each apparition in Act 4 offers false comfort. By giving Macbeth so little time to enjoy his success, Shakespeare suggests that ambition satisfied through murder destroys the very thing it wins.

**Why it works:** it names structural features (rise and fall, turning point), refers to precise moments with act and scene, and ends with a comment on what Shakespeare is suggesting.

question.text:
Read this short passage from Act 3 Scene 4, after the ghost of Banquo has vanished and the guests have left.

> MACBETH: I am in blood / Stepp'd in so far that, should I wade no more, / Returning were as tedious as go o'er.

Starting with this moment, explain how Shakespeare uses the **structure** of the play to show Macbeth's downfall. Write about:

- how this moment acts as a turning point
- how events before and after it shape our view of Macbeth's fall.
question.hint: Think about where this scene sits in the five-act structure, what Macbeth has already done, and what he goes on to do. Use the word 'turning point' or 'climax' and refer to specific later events.
question.explanation: A strong answer explains that the banquet is the climax: Macbeth has reached the throne but his guilt is exposed publicly. The blood metaphor shows he feels trapped and chooses to go on rather than repent. Before this, his crimes were planned with Lady Macbeth; after this he acts alone (the apparitions, the Macduff murders), his wife declines and dies, and the prophecies turn against him. The cyclical ending, with Macbeth beheaded like Cawdor, completes the fall.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies the banquet scene as a turning point or climax in the structure
Explains the blood image as showing Macbeth trapped or choosing to continue with violence
Refers to a relevant earlier event (Duncan's murder, the prophecy or Banquo's murder)
Refers to a relevant later event (apparitions, Macduff's family, Lady Macbeth's death, Birnam Wood)
Comments on the rise and fall shape of tragedy or the cyclical ending
Explains what Shakespeare suggests about ambition, guilt or tyranny through this structure

activities.title: Key points
activities.content:
- **Act 1**: prophecy, Cawdor, Malcolm named heir, Lady Macbeth's plan.
- **Act 2**: dagger, Duncan murdered, Porter, Macduff discovers the body, princes flee.
- **Act 3**: Banquo murdered, Fleance escapes, banquet and ghost (the **climax**).
- **Act 4**: three apparitions, eight kings, Macduff's family killed, Malcolm tests Macduff.
- **Act 5**: sleepwalking, Birnam Wood moves, Lady Macbeth dies, Macduff kills Macbeth, Malcolm crowned.
- The play is a **five-act tragedy** with a fast rise and a long fall, ending in a **cycle** back to a battle and a traitor's death.
- In essays, use plot events as **evidence**, not as a story to retell.

practiceQuestions.text: True or false: Duncan is murdered on stage in front of the audience.
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about what we actually see in Act 2 Scene 2.
practiceQuestions.explanation: False. The murder happens off stage; we only see Macbeth return with the bloody daggers, which makes the audience imagine the horror.

practiceQuestions.text: Which title does Duncan give Macbeth at the start of the play?
practiceQuestions.hint: It once belonged to a traitor.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Macbeth is made Thane of Cawdor after the previous Thane is executed for treason. He is already Thane of Glamis.

practiceQuestions.text: Put these events from the second half of the play in the correct order.
practiceQuestions.hint: The apparitions come before the murder of Macduff's family, and Lady Macbeth's sleepwalking is in Act 5.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Banquo's ghost appears in 3.4, the apparitions in 4.1, Macduff's family is killed in 4.2, Lady Macbeth sleepwalks in 5.1 and Macduff kills Macbeth in 5.8.
order: Banquo's ghost appears at the banquet
The witches show Macbeth three apparitions
Macduff's wife and children are murdered
Lady Macbeth sleepwalks and tries to wash her hands

practiceQuestions.text: Match each act to a key event that happens in it.
practiceQuestions.hint: Remember: prophecy, murder, ghost, apparitions, final battle.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Act 1: the witches' prophecy. Act 2: Duncan's murder. Act 3: Banquo's ghost. Act 4: the apparitions. Act 5: Birnam Wood moves.

pairs.right: The witches prophesy that Macbeth will be king
Banquo's ghost appears at the banquet
Birnam Wood appears to move towards Dunsinane

practiceQuestions.text: Complete the sentence about the end of the play.

metadata.blanksText: Macbeth is killed by ___, and ___ is hailed as the new King of Scotland.

practiceQuestions.hint: The killer was not born in the usual way; the new king is Duncan's elder son.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Macduff, who was born by caesarean, kills Macbeth. Malcolm, Duncan's son, becomes king.

practiceQuestions.text: Which TWO of the following are examples of prophecies that come true in an unexpected way?
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about the tricks hidden inside the apparitions' words.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Birnam Wood 'moves' because soldiers carry branches, and Macduff was not 'born' in the normal way. The Cawdor prophecy comes true straightforwardly, and Banquo never becomes king.

options.text: No man of woman born can harm Macbeth

options.feedback: This one comes true in a plain, expected way.
The prophecy is about Banquo's descendants, not Banquo himself.

practiceQuestions.text: Explain why the escape of Fleance in Act 3 Scene 3 is an important moment in the plot.
practiceQuestions.hint: Link the escape to the witches' prophecy and to Macbeth's sense of security.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Fleance's escape keeps the prophecy that Banquo's descendants will be kings alive, so Macbeth's throne is never safe. It is the first plan that fails, marking the start of his loss of control and the shift into the falling action of the play.

markScheme.criterion: Links the escape to the prophecy about Banquo's descendants becoming kings
Explains that Macbeth's position is now insecure or that he feels threatened
Identifies it as the first failure or the start of Macbeth losing control (turning point)

practiceQuestions.text: How does the ending of the play mirror its beginning?
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about what happens to the Thane of Cawdor in Act 1.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Both open and close with a battle against a traitor who is beheaded, and the loyal thane who defeats him is honoured. Macbeth ends as the traitor he replaced, creating a cyclical structure.

options.text: A traitor is defeated and beheaded, and loyal men are rewarded by the rightful king
The witches appear again to make a new prophecy
Lady Macbeth reads another letter from her husband
Duncan's ghost returns to crown Malcolm

practiceQuestions.text:
Read this short passage from Act 1 Scene 4, spoken as an aside after Duncan names Malcolm his heir.

> MACBETH: Stars, hide your fires; / Let not light see my black and deep desires.

How does Shakespeare use this moment, and the events around it in Act 1, to prepare the audience for the murder of Duncan?
practiceQuestions.hint: Consider the timing (straight after the Cawdor prophecy comes true), the aside, the light and dark imagery, and what happens next with Lady Macbeth.
practiceQuestions.explanation: A good answer notes the aside reveals hidden intent that Duncan cannot hear; the dark imagery links ambition to secrecy and evil; the timing (right after the prophecy is half-fulfilled and an obstacle appears) shows ambition turning to intent; and Lady Macbeth's reaction to the letter in the next scene turns desire into a plan.

markScheme.criterion: Makes a clear point about Macbeth's hidden or growing ambition
Analyses the aside as revealing thoughts hidden from other characters
Analyses the light and dark imagery
Refers to Malcolm being named heir as the obstacle that prompts the thought
Links forward to Lady Macbeth's plan or the murder in Act 2

practiceQuestions.text: True or false: Macbeth visits the witches a second time, of his own choice, after the banquet.
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about what Macbeth decides at the end of Act 3 Scene 4.
practiceQuestions.explanation: True. After the ghost scene he says he will go to the witches to learn more, showing he now actively seeks out the supernatural rather than simply meeting it by chance.
